questions.question: Who among the following is NOT considered a leader of the Moderates in the Indian National Congress?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Aurobindo Ghosh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Aurobindo Ghosh is primarily associated with the **Extremist faction** of the Indian National Congress, not the Moderates.
 
• He played a significant role in promoting **radical nationalism** and advocating for complete independence rather than gradual reforms.
 
• During the early 1900s, Aurobindo Ghosh emerged as a key leader of the Extremists alongside Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal.
 
• His political philosophy included the use of **passive resistance** and boycotts to oppose British rule.
 
• He later retired from active politics and shifted his focus to spirituality, establishing the **Sri Aurobindo Ashram** in Puducherry.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Moderates in the Indian National Congress**

 
 
• Moderates were a group of leaders in the Congress who believed in achieving political reforms through **constitutional and peaceful methods.**
 
• Key leaders included **Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale and Ferozshah Mehta.**
 
• Their primary aim was to secure **greater representation for Indians in the legislative councils** and administrative reforms.
 
• They often relied on **petitions, speeches, and lobbying** to achieve their goals.
 
 
 
• **Extremists in the Indian National Congress**
 
 
• Extremists were a faction within the Congress that emerged in the early 1900s, advocating for **direct action and complete independence.**
 
• Key leaders included **Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, and Lala Lajpat Rai.**
 
• They used methods like **boycotts, Swadeshi movement, and mass mobilization** to challenge British rule.
 
• The split between Moderates and Extremists occurred at the **Surat Session of the Congress in 1907.**
 
 
 
• **Dadabhai Naoroji**
 
 
• Known as the "Grand Old Man of India," Dadabhai Naoroji was a prominent Moderate leader.
 
• He authored the book **"Poverty and Un-British Rule in India,"** highlighting the economic drain caused by British policies.
 
• He was the first Indian to be elected to the British Parliament in 1892.
 
 
 
• **Gopal Krishna Gokhale**
 
 
• A Moderate leader and mentor to Mahatma Gandhi, Gokhale was a staunch advocate of **social reforms and education.**
 
• He founded the **Servants of India Society** to promote social welfare and national awakening.

questions.question: What happens to the particles of a substance when it is heated?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**They move faster**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• When a substance is heated, its particles gain **kinetic energy**, causing them to move faster.
 
• Heating increases the temperature, which directly affects the **motion of particles** in solids, liquids, and gases.
 
• In solids, the particles vibrate more vigorously around their fixed positions as the temperature rises.
 
• In liquids and gases, the particles move faster and spread out, leading to processes like **expansion** and changes in state (e.g., evaporation).
 
• This phenomenon is explained by the **Kinetic Theory of Matter**, which states that particles are in constant motion and their energy depends on temperature.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kinetic Energy:**

 
 
• The energy possessed by a particle due to its motion.
 
• It increases with temperature, causing faster movement of particles.
 
 
 
• **Expansion on Heating:**
 
 
• Substances generally expand when heated due to increased particle motion.
 
• This property is utilized in applications like **thermometers**.
 
 
 
• **Phase Changes:**
 
 
• Heating can cause substances to change state, such as solid to liquid (melting) or liquid to gas (evaporation).
 
• This occurs because particles move faster and overcome intermolecular forces.
 
 
 
• **Kinetic Theory of Matter:**
 
 
• A scientific theory explaining the behavior of particles in matter based on their kinetic energy.
 
• States that temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles.
 
 
 
• **Brownian Motion:**
 
 
• An observable phenomenon in liquids and gases where particles move randomly due to collisions.
 
• It becomes more prominent as particles gain energy from heating.

questions.question: When were privy purses officially abolished in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1971**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Privy purses were annual payments made to the rulers of erstwhile princely states as part of the integration of these states into the Indian Union post-independence.
 
• These payments were guaranteed under Articles 291 and 362 of the Indian Constitution to ensure the cooperation of princely states during the process of integration.
 
• In 1971, under the leadership of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, the 26th Amendment to the Constitution of India was enacted, officially abolishing privy purses.
 
• The 26th Amendment removed Articles 291 and 362 from the Constitution and abolished the recognition of rulers as well as their privileges.
 
• The move was part of the broader effort to promote equality and eliminate the remnants of feudalism in independent India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Privy Purses:**

 
 
• Privy purses were monetary allowances given to the rulers of princely states as part of their agreement to join India.
 
• The amount varied based on the size, revenue, and status of the princely state.
 
 
 
• **26th Constitutional Amendment:**
 
 
• This amendment was passed in 1971 and removed Articles 291 and 362 from the Indian Constitution.
 
• It ended the recognition of princely states and abolished all privileges, titles, and privy purses associated with them.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Abolition:**
 
 
• The abolition of privy purses was seen as a step toward reducing inequality and strengthening the democratic fabric of India.
 
• It also marked the end of any feudal privileges and ensured that all citizens were treated equally under the law.
 
 
 
• **Integration of Princely States:**
 
 
• Post-independence, there were more than 550 princely states in India.
 
• Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and V.P. Menon played key roles in integrating these states into the Indian Union through diplomacy and negotiation.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the ten indicators used in calculating the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Internet connectivity**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) is calculated using ten indicators across three broad dimensions: **health, education, and standard of living**.
 
• The indicators under the health dimension include **nutrition** and **child mortality**.
 
• Under the education dimension, the indicators used are **years of schooling** and **school attendance**.
 
• The standard of living dimension includes indicators such as **access to electricity**, drinking water, sanitation, cooking fuel, housing, and asset ownership.
 
• **Internet connectivity** is not one of the indicators used in calculating the MPI, as it focuses on basic needs and capabilities rather than technological access.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI):**

 
 
• Developed by the **Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI)** and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).
 
• Aims to provide a more comprehensive measure of poverty beyond just income levels.
 
• It captures the overlapping deprivations individuals or households face across multiple dimensions.
 
 
 
• **Dimensions and Indicators:**
 
 
• Health: Nutrition, Child Mortality.
 
• Education: Years of Schooling, School Attendance.
 
• Standard of Living: Cooking Fuel, Sanitation, Drinking Water, Electricity, Housing, Assets.
 
 
 
• **Global MPI Reports:**
 
 
• The MPI is included in the **Human Development Reports** released annually by the UNDP.
 
• It provides valuable insights into poverty trends and is used for policymaking and international comparisons.
 
 
 
• **Focus on Basic Needs:**
 
 
• The MPI emphasizes fundamental human needs such as health, education, and basic living standards.
 
• Technological access, including internet connectivity, is not included as it is not considered a core indicator of poverty reduction.

questions.question: A patient lacking bile production would suffer from deficiency in absorption of ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**fat-soluble vitamins**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Bile is essential for the emulsification of fats, which allows for the digestion and absorption of fat-soluble vitamins such as **Vitamins A, D, E, and K**.
 
• Without bile, fats remain undigested, and the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins in the small intestine becomes impaired.
 
• **Fat-soluble vitamins** require the presence of dietary fats and bile salts to form micelles, which facilitate their absorption into the intestinal cells.
 
• A deficiency in bile production can lead to health issues such as night blindness (Vitamin A deficiency), rickets (Vitamin D deficiency), and clotting disorders (Vitamin K deficiency).
 
• Patients with bile production issues may require medical interventions like bile supplements or dietary modifications to ensure proper nutrient absorption.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bile and Its Role:**

 
 
• Bile is produced by the liver and stored in the gallbladder, released into the small intestine during digestion.
 
• It contains bile salts, cholesterol, and waste products like bilirubin, which help in fat digestion and the excretion of waste.
 
 
 
• **Fat-Soluble Vitamins:**
 
 
• Fat-soluble vitamins include **Vitamins A, D, E, and K**, which are stored in the liver and fatty tissues for later use.
 
• These vitamins are crucial for vision (A), bone health (D), antioxidation (E), and blood clotting (K).
 
 
 
• **Micelle Formation:**
 
 
• Bile salts help in the formation of micelles, which are tiny droplets that make fats and fat-soluble vitamins soluble in the watery environment of the intestine.
 
• This process is critical for their absorption across the intestinal lining.
 
 
 
• **Diseases Linked to Bile Deficiency:**
 
 
• Conditions like gallstones, liver diseases, or bile duct obstructions can reduce bile production or flow, leading to malabsorption of fats and fat-soluble vitamins.
 
• Patients may experience symptoms like diarrhea, weight loss, and deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins.
 
 
 
• **Treatment Options:**
 
 
• Treatment may include bile acid supplements, a low-fat diet, or addressing underlying conditions like gallbladder or liver disease.
 
• Supplementation of fat-soluble vitamins is often recommended for individuals with chronic bile deficiency.

• Alauddin Khalji strengthened the fortifications of Delhi and reorganized his army to counter the Mongol threat effectively.

• **Khalji Dynasty:**

 
 
• The Khalji dynasty ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1290 to 1320 CE and marked a significant phase in Indian medieval history.
 
• Alauddin Khalji, one of the most prominent rulers, is known for his ambitious military campaigns, administrative reforms, and economic policies.
 
• He implemented strict price controls and market regulations to prevent inflation and ensure the welfare of his subjects.
 
 
 
• **Mongol Invasions:**
 
 
• The Mongols were a nomadic group originating from Central Asia, known for their expansion under leaders like Genghis Khan.
 
• They invaded northern India multiple times during the 13th and 14th centuries, driven by territorial ambition and strategic interests.
 
• The invasions caused widespread destruction, but Indian rulers like Alauddin Khalji successfully resisted their advances.
 
 
 
• **Military Reforms of Alauddin Khalji:**
 
 
• Alauddin Khalji established a standing army, known as the "Diwan-i-Arz," and introduced rigorous training and discipline.
 
• He built defensive structures like fortresses and ensured the loyalty of his commanders by providing regular salaries and rewards.
 
• These measures helped him repel external threats, including the Mongols, and maintain internal stability.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Mongol Invasions:**
 
 
• The invasions disrupted trade, agriculture, and the overall economy in northern India during the period.
 
• The Mongol raids also exposed vulnerabilities in Indian defense systems, prompting rulers to enhance military preparedness.
 
• Despite their destructive nature, the Mongols failed to establish a lasting presence in India due to effective resistance from rulers like Alauddin Khalji.

questions.question: How many recognised styles of Vedic recitation (Pathas) are there?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Eleven**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• There are **eleven recognised styles** of Vedic recitation (Pathas) in the traditional system of preserving Vedic texts.
 
• The styles of recitation are **designed to maintain the purity and accuracy** of the Vedic scriptures.
 
• Some of the well-known styles include **Samhita Patha, Pada Patha, Krama Patha, Jata Patha, and Ghana Patha**.
 
• These recitation techniques have been passed down through **oral tradition** for thousands of years, ensuring the preservation of the Vedas.
 
• The system of Vedic recitation has been recognised as a part of UNESCO's **Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Vedas and Their Significance:**

 
 
• The Vedas are the oldest sacred texts of Hinduism, comprising four main collections: Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, and Atharvaveda.
 
• They encompass hymns, rituals, and philosophical knowledge, forming the foundation of Vedic traditions.
 
 
 
• **Oral Tradition:**
 
 
• The Vedic texts were transmitted orally for centuries before being written down.
 
• The recitation techniques helped preserve their integrity despite the absence of written scripts.
 
 
 
• **Key Recitation Styles:**
 
 
• **Samhita Patha:** Continuous recitation of the text as written.
 
• **Krama Patha:** Reciting words in a sequential overlapping manner, e.g., AB, BC, CD.
 
• **Ghana Patha:** A complex style that repeats words in specific patterns for accuracy.
 
 
 
• **UNESCO Recognition:**
 
 
• In 2008, the tradition of Vedic chanting was inscribed in the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
 
• This recognition highlights its significance as one of the oldest unbroken oral traditions in the world.

questions.question: What happens when an Indian citizen renounces their citizenship?

• The individual may acquire citizenship of another country, but dual citizenship is not permitted under Indian law.

• The OCI card provides certain rights, such as visa-free travel to India and access to specific rights, but it does not confer full citizenship.
 
 
 
• **Dual Citizenship:**
 
 
• India does not allow dual citizenship under its laws.
 
• Individuals renouncing Indian citizenship may acquire citizenship of another country, but they cannot simultaneously retain Indian citizenship.

questions.question: What was the main reason for the protest against the Simon Commission in 1928?

• The lack of Indian representation in the Simon Commission highlighted the demand for greater self-governance and autonomy, fueling the freedom struggle further.

• The absence of Indian members in the Commission was seen as a deliberate exclusion, sparking national outrage.
 
 
 
• **Lala Lajpat Rai's Protest**

• **P-block elements** include non-metals, metalloids, and noble gases, but not transition elements.
 
• These elements belong to Groups **13 to 18** of the periodic table.

• The p-block includes halogens (Group 17) and noble gases (Group 18), which exhibit unique chemical properties.

• These elements are found in Groups 3 to 12 of the periodic table.
 
• Their general electronic configuration is (n-1)d¹–¹⁰ns¹–².
 
• They exhibit metallic properties and are known for forming colored compounds and acting as catalysts.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the American Standard Code for Information Interchange (ASCII)?

options.text: To design a graphical user interface for operating systems
To enable secure encryption of data for internet transmission
To create a programming language for text-based applications
To define a standardised set of codes for representing text and control characters

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To define a standardised set of codes for representing text and control characters**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange)** is a character encoding standard used to represent text in computers, telecommunications, and other devices.
 
• Developed in the **1960s**, ASCII assigns a unique numerical value (0-127) to **letters, digits, punctuation marks, and control characters**.
 
• It enables universal **data exchange between different types of devices and software** by standardizing text representation.
 
• The ASCII standard includes **128 characters**, with codes 0-31 reserved for control characters (e.g., newline, tab) and codes 32-127 for printable characters.
 
• ASCII remains the foundation for many modern encoding systems, including **UTF-8 and Unicode**, which build upon it for broader character support.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Character Encoding:** Character encoding is the process of assigning a numerical value to each character, enabling computers to store and manipulate text.
 
• **Control Characters:** ASCII codes 0-31 are reserved for non-printable control characters, such as **newline (code 10)** and **tab (code 9)**.
 
• **Extended ASCII:** Extended ASCII expands the standard 128 characters to include 256 characters, incorporating additional symbols, accents, and graphical elements.
 
• **Unicode:** Unicode is a universal character encoding system that supports over 140,000 characters across multiple languages and scripts, building upon ASCII for broader compatibility.
 
• **Usage in Computing:** ASCII codes are widely used in programming, data transfer, and storage to ensure compatibility across systems.

questions.question: What happens if a law is declared unconstitutional under judicial review?

options.text: It is sent back to the Parliament for reconsideration.
It is amended by the President

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It becomes null and void.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• If a law is declared unconstitutional under judicial review, it **ceases to have any legal effect** and is treated as if it never existed.
 
• The judiciary exercises this power under the principle of **constitutional supremacy**, ensuring that all laws adhere to the constitution.
 
• Such a declaration is binding on all authorities, including the legislature, executive, and judiciary.
 
• The law is considered **null and void** from the date of its enactment, unless the court specifies otherwise.
 
• This power of judicial review is a key feature of democracies like India and the USA, ensuring the protection of **fundamental rights** and constitutional integrity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Judicial Review:**

 
 
• It is the power of the judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative and executive actions.
 
• Judicial review ensures that no law or government action violates the constitution.
 
• In India, this power is derived from Articles 13, 32, and 226 of the Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Unconstitutional Law:**
 
 
• A law is termed unconstitutional when it contravenes the provisions of the constitution, particularly fundamental rights.
 
• Such laws cannot be enforced and lose their legal validity.
 
 
 
• **Doctrine of Basic Structure:**
 
 
• The judiciary uses this doctrine to ensure that amendments or laws do not alter the basic framework of the constitution.
 
• This doctrine was established in the landmark Kesavananda Bharati case (1973).
 
 
 
• **Article 13 of the Indian Constitution:**
 
 
• Article 13 declares that any law inconsistent with the fundamental rights shall be void.
 
• It forms the basis for judicial review in India.

questions.question: When was the protection and improvement of environment and safeguarding of forests and wildlife as a directive added in the Constitution of India?

__
 
• The protection and improvement of the environment and safeguarding forests and wildlife were added as **Directive Principles of State Policy** under Article 48A of the Indian Constitution in **1976**.
 
• This amendment was made through the **42nd Constitutional Amendment Act**, which is considered one of the most extensive amendments in Indian constitutional history.
 
• Article 48A directs the State to endeavor to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wildlife of the country.
 
• Additionally, Article 51A(g) was also added through the 42nd Amendment, which makes it a fundamental duty of every citizen to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers, and wildlife.
 
• The 42nd Amendment Act was enacted during the tenure of Prime Minister **Indira Gandhi**, who emphasized environmental protection as a key priority.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP):**

 
 
• DPSPs are guidelines for the central and state governments to ensure social and economic welfare in India.
 
• They are non-justiciable, meaning they cannot be enforced by courts, but they are fundamental in governance.
 
• Environmental protection was incorporated under DPSPs through Article 48A, emphasizing sustainable development.
 
 
 
• **42nd Amendment Act of 1976:**
 
 
• It introduced significant changes to the Constitution, including adding new directives and duties.
 
• It added Articles 48A and 51A(g), focusing on environmental conservation.
 
• It is often referred to as the "Mini-Constitution" due to its sweeping impact on constitutional provisions.
 
 
 
• **Fundamental Duties:**
 
 
• Fundamental Duties were added to the Constitution through the 42nd Amendment under Article 51A.
 
• Article 51A(g) specifically states that citizens must protect and improve the environment.
 
• Fundamental Duties are non-enforceable but serve as moral obligations for Indian citizens.
 
 
 
• **Global Environmental Awareness:**
 
 
• The incorporation of environmental protection in the Indian Constitution was influenced by global movements like the **United Nations Conference on the Human Environment (1972)** held in Stockholm.
 
• India was one of the signatories to the Stockholm Declaration, which emphasized environmental conservation worldwide.

questions.question: Which factor plays the most dominant role in the seasonal reversal of wind direction in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Monsoonal pressure system**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The seasonal reversal of wind direction in India is primarily driven by the **monsoonal pressure system**, which is influenced by differential heating of land and water surfaces.
 
• During summer, intense heating of the Indian subcontinent creates a **low-pressure area over northern India**, attracting moisture-laden winds from the Indian Ocean.
 
• In winter, the land cools down rapidly, forming a **high-pressure area**, while the Indian Ocean remains relatively warm, causing winds to reverse direction.
 
• The monsoonal pressure system is a key feature of India's climate and is responsible for **seasonal rainfall patterns**, which are crucial for agriculture and water resources.
 
• This dynamic system is heavily influenced by the **Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ)**, which shifts northward during summer and southward during winter.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Monsoon Definition:** The term "monsoon" originates from the Arabic word "mausim," meaning season. It refers to the seasonal wind patterns driven by temperature and pressure differences between land and sea.
 
• **Southwest Monsoon:** Occurs during summer (June–September) when winds blow from the Indian Ocean towards the Indian subcontinent, bringing heavy rainfall.
 
• **Northeast Monsoon:** Occurs during winter (October–December) when winds reverse direction, carrying dry air from land to sea and resulting in limited rainfall in certain regions.
 
• **Role of ITCZ:** The Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone is a belt of low pressure near the equator where trade winds converge. Its north-south movement significantly impacts monsoon dynamics.
 
• **El Niño and La Niña:** These oceanic phenomena can influence monsoon intensity and rainfall patterns by affecting sea surface temperatures and atmospheric circulation.

questions.question: Which of the following characters is NOT allowed in a filename when renaming in Windows?

__
 
• The **question mark (?)** is one of the characters prohibited in filenames in Windows operating systems.
 
• Other restricted characters include **\ / : * ? " |**, as these are reserved for system functions or file path navigation.
 
• Windows uses these special characters to perform certain operations, such as separating directories (**/**) or indicating a wildcard (*****).
 
• If you attempt to include a restricted character while renaming a file, Windows will display an error message preventing the action.
 
• These restrictions are enforced to ensure compatibility and avoid conflicts within the file system.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Filename Restrictions in Windows:**

 
 
• Windows filenames cannot exceed 255 characters, including the file path.
 
• Filenames cannot end with a period (**.**) or a space (** **).
 
• Reserved names like **CON, AUX, NUL, COM1** to **COM9**, and **LPT1** to **LPT9** are also prohibited.
 
 
 
• **Wildcard Characters:**
 
 
• Wildcards like ***** and **?** are used to represent multiple or single characters in searches.
 
• Including these in filenames can interfere with file search or system commands.
 
 
 
• **File Path Syntax:**
 
 
• Windows uses **\** as a directory separator, distinguishing file paths.
 
• Other characters like **:** are reserved for drives (e.g., **C:\**).
 
 
 
• **Cross-Platform Compatibility:**
 
 
• Some characters allowed in other operating systems (e.g., Linux) may still be prohibited in Windows.
 
• Developers often avoid restricted characters to ensure portability across platforms.

questions.question: What type of coastal plain are the Western Coastal Plains of India classified as?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Submerged Coastal Plain**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Western Coastal Plains of India are classified as **submerged coastal plains**, formed due to the submergence of landmass along the western coastline.
 
• This type of plain features narrow coastal strips with lagoons, estuaries, and backwaters commonly found in regions like Kerala.
 
• The submergence of land has resulted in characteristic landforms such as **rivers flowing into the Arabian Sea forming estuaries**, unlike the deltas formed in the eastern coastal plains.
 
• Prominent features of the Western Coastal Plains include **the Konkan Coast (Maharashtra), the Malabar Coast (Kerala), and the Kannad Coast (Karnataka)**.
 
• The submerged nature of the plains makes them rich in aquatic biodiversity, supporting fisheries and other marine activities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Submerged Coastal Plain:**

 
 
• These plains are formed when coastal regions sink below sea level due to tectonic movements or rising sea levels.
 
• Submerged plains often feature estuaries, lagoons, and submerged valleys.
 
• Examples include the Western Coastal Plains of India and parts of the eastern United States coastline.
 
 
 
• **Eastern Coastal Plains vs Western Coastal Plains:**
 
 
• Eastern Coastal Plains are emergent plains, characterized by wide deltas of rivers like the Ganga, Godavari, and Krishna.
 
• Western Coastal Plains are submerged plains, with narrow coastal strips and estuaries formed by rivers flowing into the Arabian Sea.
 
 
 
• **Estuaries:**
 
 
• An estuary is a partially enclosed coastal body of water where freshwater from rivers meets and mixes with saltwater from the sea.
 
• Estuaries are rich in biodiversity and serve as critical habitats for various aquatic species.
 
 
 
• **Backwaters:**
 
 
• Backwaters are brackish lagoons or lakes lying parallel to the coast, formed due to the action of waves and tides.
 
• Kerala is famous for its extensive network of backwaters, such as Vembanad Lake.
